content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This work studies how over-parametrization smoothens the loss landscape in neural networks. The work also shows interesting negative results, notably that over-parametrized networks can have bad local minima. It clarified the notion of "bad local minima" and distinguishes between weakly global functions and non-weakly-global functions. These negative results are nice and interesting as they go again the widely accepted claim that over-parametrization makes the landscape always "nicer".

A major drawback of this work is that it completely ignores the generalization properties of the corresponding neural network. It is not at all surprising that over-parametrization makes optimization simpler. The real point to explain about over-parametrization is why at the same time it does not hurt generalization. The paper admits that it does not consider the generalization properties. But as such it is not relevant to understanding learning properties of deep neural networks.

The absence of 'bad' local minima seems particularly irrelevant in the view of recent line of work on overparametrized neural networks, shoving that best generalization properties are achieved in the so-called interpolating regime where there exist many global minima of the loss landscape, all with zero training error, but only some of them leading to good generalization. The real question is to explain why the algorithm dynamics find those that generalize well and not the other one. The present work does not shed any light on this question. 

So while I do appreciate some of the negative results I think overall this work does not constitute an important contribution to the current questions and I hence lean towards rejection. 


Minor comments: 

I am not really appreciating the analogy between illnesses of the landscape and the human body. This is maybe useful in a wide audience newspaper article, but I do not see its use here where readers are well aware of the underlying questions and concepts. Talking of “pharmacodynamics" and related does not really seem of interest. 

The article is full of misprints: last paragraph on page 1: has -> have, inima - minima 

I am also noting that the paper has 10 pages and hence according to the paper call higher standards should be applied in the review process.

display_title: Phase transition is the major result

content.title: Phase transition is the major result
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for careful reading and insightful comments. The major comment is about generalization, but our main result is "phase transition" on optimization landscape. 

(1) "it completely ignores the generalization properties of the corresponding neural network". "The real question is to explain why the algorithm dynamics find those that generalize well and not the other one."

Response: We agree that generalization is a crucial topic for DNN. However, we are still far from fully understanding the training issue, and there are many papers in the area have only studied training,  mostly for overparameterized cases: 

Du & Lee (2018); Ge et al. (2018); Andoni et al. (2014); Sedghi & Anandkumar (2014); Janzamin et al. (2015); Haeffele &Vidal (2015); Gautier et al. (2016); Brutzkus & Globerson (2017); Soltanolkotabi (2017); Soudry &Hoffer (2017); Goel & Klivans (2017); Boob & Lan (2017); Du et al. (2017); Zhong et al. (2017); Li & Yuan (2017); Liang et al. (2018a); Mei et al. (2018); Sirignano & Spiliopoulos (2018a;b);  Safran & Shamir (2018); Wang et al. (2018); Chizat & Bach (2018); Li & Liang (2018). 

All these papers ignore the generalization issue. This comment seems to be criticizing a whole subarea, and suggesting they all should be rejected?  It seems the reviewer implied optimization becomes not important recently due to recent works; we explain below.

(2) "The absence of 'bad' local minima seems particularly irrelevant "

Response: Our major negative result is the existence of "bad basins". We do prove "bad local min", but besides the math interest, it also serves the big picture of understanding why "small network is harder to train than bigger ones". 

(3) "The real question is to explain why the algorithm dynamics find those that generalize well".

Response: We kindly disagree. One of the major challenges nowadays is to train a small neural network. Many models like ResNet, BERT and BigGAN are large. It is already a hot area in empirical research, e..g, heuristic design (MobileNet,EfficientNet), network pruning Han’2015 (1510.00149), lottery ticket hypothesis (1803.03635). There are two ICLR best papers on the relation between large and small networks. But very little theory on it.

There is a fundamental question: what distinguishes small network and big networks? Smaller should generalize better, so probably NOT a generalization issue. The remaining thing is optimization. But what specific optimization issue? Bad local-min, bad basin, or saddle points, or other things? We provide the first possible answer to this question. 

We believe understanding the true optimization benefit of overparameterziation is fundamentally important, and this understanding should come from comparing with underparameterized networks.

(4) "in the view of a recent line of work on overparametrized neural networks"  "but only some of them leading to good generalization"

Response: The reviewer is thinking about "out of global-min, a subset generalizes"; we are talking about "out of local-min, only some are global-min". These are different questions. 

Whether these works really describe optimization dynamics is still not clear. For instance, Chizat et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07956 argued that they do not explain practical optimization. This is because they require at least O(n^10) neurons. Understanding O(n) schemes is still an important step towards the more challenging question of why GD generalizes (besides understanding small networks). 

==========================
Reply to the minor comments:

1. I am not really appreciating the analogy between illnesses of the landscape and the human body... Talking of “pharmacodynamics" and related does not really seem of interest. 

Response: Thank you for the comments. We feel the reviewer has not understood our main result is "phase transition", not just "bad local-min". The basic question is: what is the benefit of over-parameterization compared to under-parameterization? Many people believed "no bad local-min", but we disprove it.  Then we prove "no bad basin".

Then outsiders may feel confused: is over-parameterization good or bad? Is it a contradiction? This seems mathematically subtle. But we want to show it is not subtle; in fact, it is a simple daily life event: overparameterization eliminates one bad thing, but not all bad things. It is like medicine. 

Anyhow, after this explanation, if the reviewer still does not get the point, then we can modify it.

Further, we sincerely disagree with the comment that “readers are well aware of the underlying questions and concepts”. For example, Reviewer 2 makes mistakes at the most basic level although he “has published in this field for several years”. 

2. The article is full of misprints: last paragraph on page 1: has -> have, inima - minima 

Response: Thank you for pointing out the misprints. We will modify them and proofread the manuscript carefully.

content.title: Acknowledgement of the answer
content.comment:
I thank the authors for a detailed answer. 

(1) Please do not take me wrong, optimization is immensely important subject with relevance to many areas including learning. Yet, in connection to over-parametrization it is evident that with larger space to explore optimization will generically be simpler. This is why the part of the paper I find the most interesting is the counter-examples to that. 

"All these papers ignore the generalization issue. This comment seems to be criticizing a whole subarea" Many of them are in the one pass setting where there is no difference between training and generalization error. For the rest of them (I do not know all in detail) yes I would criticise them for the same reason.

(2) Yes, I should have written "basins". 

(3) About training small networks. What makes the authors say that "Smaller should generalize better" what is largely empirically observed is exactly the opposite "Larger generalizes better", see the recent line of work on the double-descent behaviour.

The fact that the authors define as "illness" what hurts optimization and not what hurts generalization makes me maintain my opinion that this study of very limited relevance to machine learning and ICLR.

display_title: ICLR researchers care about optimization, with best papers on the topic

content.title: ICLR researchers care about optimization, with best papers on the topic
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the quick reply. We appreciate it. 

1) " Many of them are in the one-pass setting where there is no difference between training and generalization error". Could the reviewer point out which of these mentioned papers specifically discussed generalization error? 
  The reviewer might be arguing they are dealing with "one-pass" setting, but doesn't the same criticism apply if they don't discuss generalization error?

2) Thanks for mentioning the "double descent curve". We will surely cite these papers. 
      "Smaller generalizes better" appears in double descent curve too: below a threshold which is the traditional regime, smaller generalizes better. It seems we are discussing different regimes regarding # of parameters.
      The reviewer is interested in"why generalization is good or even improves when adding parameters", we are asking "why the optimization becomes hard when deleting parameters" (like network pruning observed). There are a few segments in the double descent curve, we are dealing with the left segment ---but not exactly, as this curve does not capture what we want to talk about. 
      Part of the reasons of the reviewer's standpoint, we guess, is because double descent curve assumes every point is a global minimizer. So from 0 to O(n), the training error is decreasing; after O(n), can interpolate, then the training error is all zero. This is actually the curve of "representation error", not "training error" for a practical algorithm.
     We decompose training error = representation error + optimization error. Thus from 0 to m*, representation error decreases; after m*, all 0. For optimization error, there is an extra parameter m > m*: from m* to m, one cannot find global-min though can represent well.  In practice, m = # of practical network parameters, m* = # of parameters after network pruning. Lottery ticket hypothesis paper shows for m* parameters, though traditional training cannot find global min, using a truncated random initial point can find global min. 
      The distinction between optimization and representation error is ignored in double descent curve, and thus we kind of understand why the reviewer only sees the "generalization issue" in the curve. 

     "Why the optimization becomes hard for small models" is pursued by practitioners nowadays. There are 2 ICLR best papers  Han’16 (1510.00149) Frankel'19 (1803.03635) on this topic. In addition, Tan and Le'19 (1905.11946) says: "we have already hit the hardware memory limit, and thus further accuracy gain needs better efficiency" (means smaller models). We think these researchers would care about how to deal with the optimization of smaller models (so they also want to understand big models for this optimization purpose), in addition to generalization.  
      
      We are far from solving the problem (just like double descent curve is far from solving generalization), but we believe we are making important first steps.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper theoretically studies the benefit of overparameterization for the loss landscape in fully connected deep neural networks. Here the definition of overparameterization is the number of training samples larger than the number of neurons in a hidden layer. This paper shows that if the last hidden layer is overparameterized (with some more mild assumptions) than loss function is weakly global. This implies there are no bad strict local minima. Authors also show by example that overparameterization networks could have bad non-strict local minima could exist.

Due to last minute request, I have not been able to digest the proof so I won't be able to say anything regarding the correctness of the paper. 

While there are interesting observations one could find on overparamerized network's loss landscape,  with current form the paper's presentation is unclear and I wan not convinced on its relevance to realistic settings.  

Pros:
The paper is tackling an important question regarding the benefits of overparameterization. As authors note isolating benefits coming from overparameterization is important study.

Assumptions used to prove the theorems are general enough except for the overparameterized assumption.

Cons:
There are few problems I encountered reviewing.

I found paper unclear to read and understand. Maybe due to last minute submission, the paper does not appear to be polished and needs more work making the presentation clear.  Beyond various typos, broken reference (unnecessary Yu et al. infront of Yu & Chen (1995)), I did not find section 2 from 1-dimensional case especially helpful for understanding impact of the paper. Also since various previous works have similar claims to this paper, it would be clear to distinguish how current results are distinguished in the contribution section. For example as authors say Nguyen et al (2018)/ Venturi et al (2018) also show that non-existence of bad strict local minima. The contribution section may become clear if authors could describe specific contributions beyond what already have been described in literature. Is the relaxation to continuous activation function that is significant for example?

I have concerns about the applicability of the results. For example, in realistic data would A3 or B1 hold? For example with 50k MNIST, one would need 50k hidden layer and the benefit of overparameterization in practice appears for much smaller networks.  Also for Theorem 2 assumption B2 is quite strict which doesn’t include ReLU/TanH/Sigmoid activation functions. 

For applicability, I wonder if there would be a practical guidance based on findings in the paper which would make the results more impactful. 

While it is important to understand what type of minima overparameterization network brings in, wouldn’t more relevant true phenomenology of deep networks would be captured through statistical arguments in terms of how likely our initialization and optimization algorithm would fall into a certain type of minima. I was not convinced some of the particular examples in low dimensional settings reflects what realistic over/under parameterized neural networks are showing. 

Questions and Comments:
How is counter example in section 6.1 an example of overparameterized case? I only see one hidden unit with 1 data point which is not overparameterized by paper’s definition. 

Please remove unnecessary “Yu et al.”

Typo p1 last paragraph “has -> have”

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4 (Part I)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and helpful suggestions. As for the typos and broken references, we will modify them in our next version. For other questions and comments, we would like to make some clarifications and explanations.
 
--“I did not find section 2 from 1-dimensional case especially helpful for understanding impact of the paper.”

Comment: The 1-dim case is important for the following reason. How to judge the quality of a theoretical paper? Strong result, strong math technique, and nice intuition. Sec. 2 provides the intuition.

We have seen many colleagues asking: what is the intuition? They cannot understand the results because it is hard to “imagine” high-dimensional space. Our message is simple and clean: look at Figure 2 -- it illustrates the major insight of the paper. We feel it fascinating when we realized the general landscape can be simply described by the 1-dim case. This is often a sign of “good science”.  

More details of the example are given below. in Section 2.1, we point out that the activation functions have an impact on “whether bad local minima exist”, so for neural networks with general activation functions, we need to pursue “no bad basins” instead of “no bad local minima”. In Section 2.2, we point out that over-parameterization is the deciding factor on “whether bad basins exist”. As for the impact of the paper, we have discussed in Section 1.1.
 
--“Since various previous works have similar claims to this paper, it would be clear to distinguish how current results are distinguished in the contribution section. … Is the relaxation to continuous activation function that is significant for example?”

Answer: Yes, it is significant.

1.We first highlight: this is the first paper that proves phase transition from under to overparameterized. None of the previous papers conveys this message. Phase transition is often considered strong theoretical result. 

2.  Venturi et al (2018) considers 2-layer nets, while we consider deep nets, thus is not comparable. Nguyen et al (2018) considers smooth strictly increasing activations for deep nets, thus it is the closest. But it does not show phase transition, and it does not cover the ReLU, leaky ReLU, swish, polynomial, etc. 

3. Why important to understand all activations? The major reason is: they are of interest to many researchers in the area. 

  a) Just for ReLU, there are many papers ([Swirszcz et. al. 2016], [Zhou and Liang 2017], [Safran and Shamir 2018], [Venturi et. al. 2018], [Liang et. al. 2018]) and most are negative. We provide arguably the first positive result on deep ReLU network. 

  b) For leaky ReLU, there is a concurrent submission on non-smooth activations  https://openreview.net/forum?id=B1x6BTEKwr  that provides negative result. 

  c). Polynomial activations: concurrent submission https://openreview.net/pdf?id=rkxsgkHKvH and a recent work https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.12207v1.pdf . Again, these are covered by our paper. 

  d). Quadratic: a bunch of recent works [Soltanolkotabi et. al. 1707.04926], [Du and Lee 1803.01206]. 

Our results apply to all activations, complementary to all these works. 

4. Another two reasons why extending to continuous activations are important.

  a). Increasing activations leads to better landscape than non-increasing activations. Thus analyzing increasing activations does not fully show the power of over-parameterization.

  b). Historically, extension on activations is considered important. E.g. [Hornik’91] proved universal approximation theorem for general activations while there exist many results on strictly increasing activations in [Cybenko’89], [Hornik et al.’89], and still got published.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4 (Part II)
content.comment:
--“I have concerns about the applicability of the results. For example, in realistic data would A3 or B1 hold?”

Answer: Assumption A3 and B1 hold for many realistic networks, for example, VGG, Inception, SqueezeNet, Enet, GoogLeNet and so on. Each of these networks has a very wide layer with O(N) neurons, where N is the number of data samples, and hence A3 holds. Further, each of such wide layer is followed by a pyramid structure, where each hidden layer is followed by a narrower layer, and hence B1 also holds.
 
--“Also for Theorem 2 assumption B2 is quite strict which doesn’t include ReLU/TanH/Sigmoid activation functions.”

Comment: We kindly disagree. It includes ReLU, Tanh and Sigmoid activation functions. Assumption B2 only requires the activation function (in the pyramid structure) to be non-increasing or non-decreasing. 

We kindly point out that if the reviewer thinks including ReLU is important, then it is a “yes” answer to the previous comment “is extending to general activations important?”, and thus our results are strong. 
 
--“I wonder if there would be a practical guidance based on findings in the paper which would make the results more impactful.” 

Yes. We mentioned lottery ticket hypothesis, and we’d like to elaborate.

One of the major challenges nowadays is to train a small neural network. Many models like ResNet, BERT and BigGAN are large. A small model is very useful in mobile devices, and more accessible. It is already a hot area in empirical research, e.g., network pruning Han’2015 (1510.00149), lottery ticket hypothesis (1803.03635). These two papers won ICLR best papers, but there is very little theory on it.

There is a fundamental question: why is small network harder to train? The success of network pruning means it is not due to representation power. Smaller should generalize better, so not generalization. The remaining thing is optimization. But what specific optimization issue? Bad local-min, bad basin, saddle points, or other things? We provide the first answer to this. 

The empirical guidance is: when designing architecture, we should try to eliminate basins. When designing algorithms, we should try to escape basins. Specific methods are left to future research.

--“While it is important to understand what type of minima over-parameterization network brings in, wouldn’t more relevant true phenomenology of deep networks would be captured through statistical arguments in terms of how likely our initialization and optimization algorithm would fall into a certain type of minima.”

Comment: It is a very interesting question, but difficult for deep neural-nets. This is basically a more precise “map” of the landscape. We are describing what local minima exist and what do not, which is an important first step.

Somewhat related to your question, lottery ticket hypothesis showed a special truncating-initialization leads to better results than random initial point. But it is not “statistical”, and not theoretical. 

--“I was not convinced some of the particular examples in low dimensional settings reflects what realistic over/under parameterized neural networks are showing.”

Comment: We indeed proved that the property of “no bad basin” exists for any dimension, not just low-dim. What does the reviewer mean by ”not convinced”? This comment is quite confusing to us. 
 
--“How is counter example in section 6.1 an example of over-parameterized case? I only see one hidden unit with 1 data point which is not over-parameterized by paper’s definition.”

Answer: Our paper’s definition of “over-parameterization” is d>=N. In example 1 there are d>=1 hidden neurons, and N =1 data point, so it is overparameterized.
 
Again, we thank the reviewer for the detailed comments and helpful suggestions. We hope our clarifications and explanations will convey a deeper understanding of our main ideas and major contributions.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper discusses the effects of over-parameterization in deep neural networks. The main claim is that for any continuous activation function the loss function does not have so-called “setwise strict“ local minima, i.e., one can find a path to the global minimum without increasing the energy along the path. The main assumption is that if the number of datapoints is N, the activation function has derivatives up to N^th order and there exists at least one layer in the network with at least N neurons. The paper seems to build upon the theory of weakly global functions which are functions for which all setwise strict local minima are setwise global minima.

This paper should be rejected for the following reasons:

1. The main claim of the paper is not true. It contradicts previously published results, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01540
2. The development in this paper is not at all rigorous. I do not see a proof of the claim. The main narrative consists of a host of special cases and elementary examples. The appendix is complicated with more special cases, e.g., Appendix D, proposition 3 is for a 1-dimensional input and one hidden layer. I do not follow the proofs for the claims in Appendix E.

I would encourage the authors to make their main narrative self-contained.

display_title: Some comments not correct; clarifications on rigorous

content.title: Some comments not correct; clarifications on rigorous
content.comment:
1. "The main claim is contradictory to https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01540." 

We kindly point out that this comment is not correct. First, these two papers consider quite different settings. In particular, they consider population risk with an extra regularization term, while ours considers empirical risk without regularization. 

Second, the conclusions are not contradictory, even ignoring the difference in settings. They prove connected sub-level set, which does not exclude the existence of bad local-min (thus no contradiction), and is consistent with "no bad basin" (thus no contradiction).

2a. “The development is not at all rigorous.”. 

We kindly disagree with "not rigorous". In fact, we have provided corresponding proofs for every claim we made. 

Due to the following comments, we suspect the reviewer wants to say "not easy to follow the proof". However, it is different from "not rigorous". 

2b. "The main narrative consists of a host of special cases and elementary examples."

Thanks for pointing it out. Only Section 2 is devoted to special cases.  Sec. 2.1 is for positive results, and Sec. 2.2 is for negative results. The special cases are to build intuition. Most readers will not read the proofs anyways, and we believe the readers can gain some intuition.  We explained that deep linear networks and deep over-parameterized networks have major properties captured by 1-dim case. We find colleagues who like this intuition. 

We can delete Sec. 2 or put to Appendix, if the reviewer thinks this is better.  
    
2c "The appendix is complicated with more special cases, e.g., Appendix D, proposition 3 is for a 1-dimensional input and one hidden layer. I do not follow the proofs for the claims in Appendix E."

Our proof consists of two steps. In Appendix D we prove the theorem for single hidden layer model, then in Appendix E we generalize the proof to deep networks by extending the key lemmas, proposition and theorem. Therefore, Appendix D not only proves the single-hidden-layer case, but also includes the main proof idea. Therefore, to fully understand the proof, we sincerely suggest the reviewer to read Appendix D before Appendix E.   

We believe these are minor issues of writing and do not make the results non-rigorous. We thank the reviewer for mentioning these, and help us improve the writing.

content.title: Restating our contributions
content.comment:
We would like to restate the main contributions of our paper.

1. Our result is the first one to demonstrate the phase transition from under- to over-parameterization. Specifically, we show that bad basins exist in under-parameterized neural networks, but are eliminated in over-parameterized neural networks. Note that phase transition is often considered strong theoretical result, but none of the previous papers conveys this message. 

The characterization of this phase transition is important. The training of small networks has become one of the major challenges nowadays. Many successful models like ResNet, BERT and BigGAN are large. Designing small and practical networks is already a hot area in empirical research, e.g, heuristic design (MobileNet, EfficientNet), network pruning Han’2015 (1510.00149), lottery ticket hypothesis (1803.03635). There are two ICLR best papers on the relation between large and small networks. But very little theory on it. There is a fundamental question: what distinguishes small network and big networks? It is likely that smaller networks generalize better, so probably NOT a generalization issue. The remaining thing is optimization. But what specific optimization issue? Bad local-min, bad basin, or saddle points, or other things? We provide the first possible answer to this question.

2. For over-parameterized neural networks, we show that bad basins do not exist for all continuous activation functions. In contrast, most existing results consider special types of activations.

We note that the assumption of continuous activations is crucial. To demonstrate the existence of phase transition, it is crucial to avoid other possible influencing factors like activation functions. Also, increasing activations leads to better landscape than non-increasing activations. Thus, analyzing increasing activations does not fully show the power of over-parameterization.

3. We correct a misconception that Property PT does not imply “no bad local minima”. Due to this misconception, the field has been too optimistic on the landscape of over-parameterized networks. Thus, our paper provides a correct understanding, which is necessary for further research and application.

Combining all points above, our paper reveals benefits of over-parameterization alone: eliminating bad basins. Our result is accurate and comprehensive, and it makes a further step in a deeper understanding of small networks.

replying_to: Replying to WHAT ILLNESS OF LANDSCAPE CAN OVER-PARAMETERIZATION ALONE CURE?

content.title: Withdrawal Statement
content.comment:
Dear all,

We are withdrawing our submission of “What Illness of Landscape can Over-parameterization Cure” from ICLR for the following reasons: 1. Due to the unfortunate review process, our work did not receive sufficient respect from the reviewers. 2. We feel that a comprehensive work that requires deeper understanding is somewhat difficult to be reviewed here. 

We received three reviews. The only reviewer who “has published in this area for several years” was making mistakes at the most basic level. The other two reviewers ”have not published in this area“, which matches the widely-discussed fact that “47% of the reviewers have not published in this area in this ICLR” but is unfortunate. They might be a bit biased in our line of research. 
     
     The reviewers did not understand the efforts and struggles over a long time to get this work done. Since they did not know the area well and did not know "many papers" we cited. 
(1) For a long time, we thought we could extend a classical work Yu,Chen'95 to prove no bad local-min. No one pointed out before. The area could be misled by this like us. We finally addressed it, in a quite comprehensive and fundamental way.  
(2) For a long time, we did not know how to get a positive clean result on ReLU networks. With a smart trick built by another paper, and a "dense activation" argument of us, we achieved a result of "any continuous activation" --which we did not even expect before.
(3) For a long time, we did not know whether bad basins exist for neural-nets or not. We even thought about proving "no bad basins exist" for any network. Nevertheless, we finally got the first general contruction of basins.
(4) This provides a clean rigorous result of "phase transition". Theoreticians should know "phase transition" is often very important. 
     
Landscape analysis of neural networks has been very popular in recent years. One popular trend is to prove positive results for a certain problem. These works might provide some intuition why neural networks can work, but they are far from explaining real networks and may cause misconceptions since the effectiveness might come from the special setting of the problem instead of neural nets themselves. Our paper, in contrast, endeavors to explore a setting that is as broad as possible. Specifically, we discover the phase transition between over-parameterized and under-parameterized networks, and we point out the exact benefit of over-parameterization alone in neural nets with both positive and negative results. Due to the broad setting and the comprehensive results, our paper is mathematically profound and technically involved, so we actually expected that the main ideas would not be that easy for the reviewers to digest. However, the reviews are still beyond our expectation as the reviewers even did not attempt to understand our major contributions. Some reviewers even gave up taking our paper seriously by simply claiming that our result is wrong using random reasons.

We still want to speak out our viewpoints. People tend to be in favor of direct results that proves “something works” instead of results that are not direct but shed lights on deeper understanding. As a result, the whole field is being too optimistic. For example, given so many positive results in the optimization power of neural networks in recent years, many people are over-confident that we can easily achieve global minimum with zero loss when training neural networks. This is far from the truth. Optimization is still a big issue, and there is barely deep understanding in it. Some misconceptions have even existed for more than 20 years. (In particular, we have corrected one in this paper. We may have also corrected another important misconception in our new paper “Sub-Optimal Local Minima Exist for Almost All Over-parameterized Neural Networks”, which is available very recently on arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01413 .) 

To this end, we, genuinely, truthfully and sincerely, call for deeper and more comprehensive understanding in the whole society, especially in the optimization of neural networks. More and more researchers are stepping forward to tackle further issues like generalization, but without deep understanding, optimization is gradually becoming a bottleneck in this field. Neural networks are definitely not omnipotent, and we need to understand the limitations for better design and training of neural networks. Results that make steps into unexplored settings or settings that are currently not working may not seem to have a direct impact immediately, but they provide cornerstones as we finally need to understand the issues, and solve them. We are not supposed to evade problems.

So many things still don’t work, but we don’t know why. Ironically, people are sticking on working things all of the time.

Sincerely,
Authors
